title: POLARIS: The Distributed SQL Engine in Azure Synapse (PVLDB 13(12), 2020)

claims.text: Polaris is Microsoft's cloud-native distributed SQL query engine, originally built for Azure Synapse, with two design goals: converge data-warehouse and big-data workloads on one engine, and fully separate compute from state so execution is stateless and elastically scalable.

Polaris abstracts every dataset as a grid of data cells indexed on two dimensions: a user-defined partition function used for aggressive partition pruning under range or equality predicates, and a system-chosen hash-distribution function that maps rows to many buckets so cells (and therefore computation) can be spread across arbitrarily many compute nodes.

The cell abstraction makes the distributed query processor storage-agnostic: the DQP operates only at cell granularity while single-node extraction of data inside a cell is delegated to the local execution engine, letting the same scale-out framework query analytical stores (ADLS, Parquet, Delta) and transactional stores alike.

Polaris compute is stateless because all durable state — data, metadata, and transaction logs — is externalized to remote storage and centralized highly-available services; only caches live on compute nodes, and since caches can be rebuilt lazily from persisted data their loss never fails in-flight work, enabling partial query restarts and online topology changes.

Query compilation in Polaris is two-phase: the SQL Server Cascades optimizer first generates the logical search space (MEMO), then a distributed cost-based phase enumerates physical distributed plans, using distribution properties both as correctness filters (e.g., an inner join requires hash-aligned inputs or a broadcast side) and as System-R-style interesting properties, and picks the plan that minimizes data movement.

Polaris injects 'data move enforcer' operators — hash re-distribution and broadcast — to change a dataset's distribution properties; enforcers are blocking, must persist all output cells before consumers start, and the operator subtree rooted at an enforcer defines the input/output boundary of a task.

A Polaris task is the physical execution of an operator expression over one hash-distribution of its inputs and has three components: input cell collections, a task template (the code for the expression), and an output cell collection; a query plan therefore becomes a DAG of task templates whose edges encode dataflow and precedence constraints.

Polaris deliberately makes tasks maximal units of work (e.g., fusing multiple hash-aligned joins into one task) and re-encodes each task template back into T-SQL that runs natively in a SQL Server instance on the compute node, so the engine combines big-data style scale-out with SQL Server's mature scale-up columnar execution, and the blocking task boundaries let SQL Server re-optimize with fresh statistics on intermediate results.

Polaris orchestrates execution as a hierarchical composition of finite state machines over entities (query DAG, task templates, tasks) with simple states like Ready/Failed/Success and composite states like Run/Blocked; transient failures are retried at task granularity and escalate to the parent state machine only if not retriable, and all transitions are logged for reproducibility and resumable execution.

Polaris schedules across queries using a global 'workload graph' that unions the task DAGs of all active queries; each task carries a multi-dimensional resource demand vector (CPU and memory are stretchable, local temp disk is rigid), compute nodes are modeled as multi-dimensional resource bins, and supported policies include FIFO, sorting by resource demand, and sorting by proximity to the DAG root to free shared resources sooner.

Task placement in Polaris is affinitized to compute by consistently assigning the same data cells to the same nodes, preserving SQL Server buffer-pool and local SSD caches across topology changes: shrinking the topology loses only the caches of removed nodes, and growing it preserves all existing caches while only new nodes warm up.

The Polaris paper demonstrates scale with two reported experiments: all 22 TPC-H queries executed at 1 PB on a pool of 420 execution nodes (the heaviest joins, Q9 and Q21, finishing in under two hours), and 5,000 concurrent TPC-DS sessions on just 10 compute nodes completing roughly 550,000 instantiated tasks with up to about 9,000 tasks packed concurrently.
